raw: 8.2 Bulk Collection, Metadata Analysis, and Legal Frameworks
teaching_note: Metadata describes attributes such as timing or endpoints, but 'not content' does not mean non-sensitive, anonymous, or unrestricted; patterns can expose relationships even without message text. **Completed synthetic disposition:** instructor policy P1, a fictional classroom rule dated 1 October 2026 rather than real law, permits processing invented minute-level timestamps for a timing exercise and prohibits sharing endpoint identifiers. The provided packet contains a timestamp, endpoint field, and unrelated message text: the reviewer retains the permitted timestamp in the exercise copy, redacts the endpoint from dissemination, and withholds the unnecessary text from analysis. On challenge, the packet lacks its acquisition-authority entry: the reviewer holds the entire packet against further use or distribution and asks the authorized instructor to resolve it, preserving or disposing of originals only under the approved rule. ICD standards do not supply collection authority or a universal retention/deletion rule; actual jurisdiction, instrument version, stage, purpose, and reviewer must be established separately.
title: Metadata and Minimization: Unknown Authority Requires a Hold

raw: 8.3 The Cryptographic Arms Race: E2E Encryption and Lawful Access
teaching_note: Confidentiality limits who can read content; integrity concerns modification; authentication binds an asserted origin to a credential/key under stated trust assumptions; provenance records the content's lineage; none proves factual truth. End-to-end encryption describes where content is protected and decrypted, not a blanket guarantee about compromised endpoints, metadata, integrity in every construction, or legal immunity. A bare hash only supports a comparison when the reference and comparison process are trustworthy; a signature requires a trusted key/signatory relationship and does not certify the statement's accuracy [@official_nist_fips_186_5_dss]. 'Lawful access' describes a legal/policy question, not proof that a technically secure access mechanism exists or that any named actor has authority. Inherited ICD citations support reasoning duties, not cryptographic security or the legality of a particular access demand.
title: Encryption, Integrity, Authentication, and Lawful-Access Claims

raw: 8.4 Covert Communications Tradecraft: OTPs, Burst Transmission, Digital Dead Drops[^27][^28]
teaching_note: The inherited list combines an encryption concept (one-time pad), a transmission-duration concept (burst transmission), and an indirect-transfer arrangement (digital dead drop); they answer different questions and do not imply the same security property. The theoretical secrecy associated with a one-time pad depends on stringent assumptions about key randomness, secrecy, length, and non-reuse, and does not by itself authenticate content or solve distribution. A short transmission or indirect delivery likewise does not establish confidentiality, anonymity, or truth. These are conceptual contrasts only; the narrow inherited sources do not validate a general secure-communications recipe, and no encoding, deployment, concealment, or evasion procedure is taught.
title: Historical Communications Concepts: Distinct Properties, No Construction Instructions

raw: 8.5 Radio Frequency Intelligence (RFINT) and Technical Surveillance[^43][^44]
teaching_note: RF describes a portion of the electromagnetic spectrum; the inherited RFINT label and vendor material should not be treated as a universally standardized intelligence discipline or a finding about a real emitter. An RF observation is not automatically communications content, a device identity, hostile intent, or evidence of surveillance. The Granite Island Group ten-level taxonomy and claimed roughly tenfold growth in detection difficulty are attributed vendor characterizations, not an independently measured universal scale; the supplied material defines no validated common difficulty metric. Keep vendor claims distinct from independently established performance and do not select frequencies, monitor transmissions, or inspect real facilities.
title: RF Evidence and Technical-Surveillance Claims: Observations versus Attribution

raw: 8.6 Technical Surveillance Countermeasures (TSCM): Threat Levels and Detection[^45][^46]
teaching_note: TSCM concerns defensive assessment of technical-surveillance risk; it is not synonymous with SIGINT collection or a particular detector. The cited service pages describe their vendors' inspection offerings, not independent estimates of sensitivity, coverage, or the probability that a space is free of devices. A supplied inspection summary saying 'no anomaly observed' supports only that stated result under its documented scope, not 'no surveillance exists'; an anomaly can also have ordinary equipment or environmental explanations. Classroom review evaluates report scope, provenance, limitations, and unresolved questions without performing sweeps, instrument deployment, interception, or live-facility assessment.
title: TSCM: Defensive Inspection Literacy and Detection Limits

raw: 8.7 Non-Linear Junction Detectors, RF Spectrum Analysis, Infrared Imaging
teaching_note: Preserve the technical modifier **non-linear**: a non-linear junction detector concerns non-linear electronic junction responses, RF spectrum analysis concerns radio-frequency energy characteristics, and infrared imaging concerns emitted/received thermal radiation patterns. These are different observation modalities, not interchangeable proof of a hidden hostile device. In wholly invented report cards, a junction response could come from ordinary electronics, an RF peak from permitted equipment, and a warm patch from a benign heat source; none alone proves surveillance or its absence. The inherited STIX/TAXII/ATLAS sources do not establish instrumentation definitions or performance, so no sensitivity, range, completeness, or deployment claim is supported here. This is device-class literacy only, with no instrument settings, search sequence, sweeps, or real-facility use.
title: Non-Linear Junction Detectors, RF Spectrum Analysis, and Infrared Imaging: Limits

raw: 8.8 Steganography: LSB, DCT, and Network-Layer Methods[^28]
teaching_note: Steganography aims to conceal the existence of a message within another carrier, whereas encryption principally protects intelligibility; neither property establishes the message's truth. LSB means least-significant bit, a low-order part of a numerical image representation; DCT means discrete cosine transform, a frequency-coefficient representation used in image processing, while network-layer approaches concern communication structures. These terms distinguish carrier representations only: the narrow cited network paper does not validate the entire taxonomy or any detector's efficacy. **Synthetic claim audit:** a fictional detector flags a recompressed image, but its card supplies no ground truth, false-positive rate, or matched benign controls; recompression is a plausible ordinary explanation, so the completed result is 'hidden content undetermined,' not proof of a payload. A later unflagged copy cannot prove absence, so hold attribution or adverse inference; no payload hiding, encoding, extraction, evasion, or real-network exercise is included.
title: Steganography: Existence-Hiding Concepts and Detection Uncertainty

teaching_note: **Completed synthetic assurance case:** supplied verification card V1 says document D1's signature is valid under a stipulated trusted course key, while D1 says a fictional exhibition opens Friday; independent supplied timetable T1 says Saturday. The signature supports the key/signature and modification check, not Friday's truth, so the analyst marks the opening date disputed and holds a definitive announcement rather than overriding T1. Clip C1 looks authentic but has no origin record or verification result, so appearance and a hypothetical detector score cannot establish speaker identity, provenance, or content accuracy; if key trust is later withdrawn, downgrade D1's authentication status too. Preserve the original, supplied checks, assumptions, conflict, and correction separately, and refer consequential reuse to the authorized instructor without contacting real people. The inherited AI/HUMINT commentary does not validate authentication capability; the signature standard supports only its bounded cryptographic properties [@official_nist_fips_186_5_dss].
title: Deepfake-Era Authentication: Valid Credentials Can Carry False Content
